items.title: Hanwha Highlights M38/M48 MUSV and Containerized Munitions at AUSA 2026
items.originalTitle: Hanwha Highlights M38/M48 MUSV and Containerized Munitions at AUSA 2026
items.summary: At AUSA 2026, Hanwha Defense USA featured a model of the M38 MUSV made in partnership with Magnet Defense, with the parent design vessel recently arriving at National Harbor just outside of Washington D.C. following previous rounds of testing at sea. Hanwha’s Kevin Schoonover provided insight into the ongoing program, including several of Hanwha’s munitions offering destined to outfit the vessel and other platforms, alongside greater detail pertaining to the partnership with Magnet Defense.

evidenceRecords.text: At AUSA 2026, Hanwha Defense USA featured a model of the M38 MUSV made in partnership with Magnet Defense, with the parent design vessel recently arriving at National Harbor just outside of Washington D.C. following previous rounds of testing at sea.

Hanwha’s Kevin Schoonover provided insight into the ongoing program, including several of Hanwha’s munitions offering destined to outfit the vessel and other platforms, alongside greater detail pertaining to the partnership with Magnet Defense.
Schoonover also highlighted how the M38 is the primary testing vehicle for the class standing at 38 meters long, with future production upgrading to the larger 48 meter standard found on the M48.
To this end steel has been cut for the first M48, with production coinciding with continued testing of the original M38.
Naval News previously reported on the partnership between Hanwha and Magnet Defense , primarily geared towards breaching the emerging U.S. USV market.
Like similar sized USVs, the M38 also features the capability to carry containerized payloads related to multiple missions, including strike, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare.
M38 has already demonstrated its range of 17,000 nautical miles on multiple tests, including a trip across the Pacific to American Samoa in up to conditions of Sea State 9 .
This has been part of a bid to introduce the M38 to overseas markets, including those beyond the U.S.’s MUSV program and Korean operation.
M38’s Weapons A scale model of the 40 foot containerized version of K-VLS II at Hanwha’s AUSA booth.
Joining the M38 at Hanwha’s booth, the company showcased offerings for both containerized Multiple Launch Rocket Systems (MLRS) and containerized Vertical Launch Systems (VLS).

When paired with M38, the vessel can carry up to 4 of the 20 foot long containerized munition packages, 2 of the 40 foot long options, or a combination of a pair of 20 foot containers and a singular 40 foot container A containerized version of the Chunmoo family of MLRS systems constitutes one of the 20 foot options, utilizing the same munitions and launch mechanisms found on the truck based version.

items.title: Ukraine is building a patchwork antiballistic defense, one stopgap at a time
items.originalTitle: Ukraine is building a patchwork antiballistic defense, one stopgap at a time
items.summary: Kyiv is assembling a patchwork of antiballistic air defense solutions, each piece on a different clock: Rounds transferred from allied stocks for this winter, imported systems and licensed production that will begin to matter over the next several years, and Freyja, a Ukrainian-European interceptor still in development. Stockpile swaps The fastest fix depends on allies sharing existing stockpiles, a request Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara put forward at his first Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting with allies on Sept. 8.

items.title: India sells air defense missiles to Tajikistan, Turkmenistan in Central Asia push
items.originalTitle: India sells air defense missiles to Tajikistan, Turkmenistan in Central Asia push
items.summary: NEW DELHI — India has sold its homegrown, short-range surface-to-air missile system called Akash, to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan gaining a foothold in Central Asia as it seeks to expand its defense exports. Analysts say these countries are turning to India to reduce their reliance on Russia, one of the region’s main arms suppliers, whose defense resources are strained by its war with Ukraine.

evidenceRecords.text: NEW DELHI — India has sold its homegrown, short-range surface-to-air missile system called Akash, to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan gaining a foothold in Central Asia as it seeks to expand its defense exports.
Analysts say these countries are turning to India to reduce their reliance on Russia, one of the region’s main arms suppliers, whose defense resources are strained by its war with Ukraine.

“They are looking for a way to diversify at a time when Russia is no longer active in defense markets as it increasingly looks inwards towards its domestic needs, reducing its capacity to export air defense systems, especially in large numbers,” Aleksei Zakharov, a fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi told Defense News.

“As a result, Central Asian countries are looking for possible alternatives.” Indian Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the sales of the Akash surface-to-air missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan earlier this month in an interview with news agency Asian New International.
India moves closer to a homegrown, long-range air defense In 2022, Armenia became India’s first foreign customer for the air defense system.
The Akash system can simultaneously engage multiple targets at ranges up to 25km according to the Defense Ministry.
Calling the system one of India’s “success stories,” Singh said: “It shows the maturing of our indigenous missile design and production system.

Confidence in the missile system got a boost after it was “battle-tested” in a real conflict, according to Zakharov and could encourage Central Asian buyers to consider other Indian hardware, such as artillery and radar systems, as growing geopolitical uncertainty prompts countries to broaden their supplier base.
“Certainly this can be an important first step for India’s entry into the defense markets of Central Asia.

“The Indian systems such as Akash are also cost-effective.” In fact, Armenia has emerged as India’s largest buyer of military equipment, signing defense contracts worth nearly $2 billion since 2020, according to reports.
Analysts say India’s outreach in Central Asia also aims to balance China’s growing influence in the region where Beijing has emerged as a major supplier of military equipment in recent years.

items.title: European U740 Variant Of The XQ-58A Valkyrie Has Flown
items.originalTitle: European U740 Variant Of The XQ-58A Valkyrie Has Flown
items.summary: Airbus and Kratos Defense & Security Solutions have completed the first flight of the U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft, a Europeanized version of the XQ-58A Valkyrie , advancing their bid to deliver a combat-ready system to Germany by 2029. The flight comes as the German Air Force, or Luftwaffe, moves toward acquiring a new class of jet-powered combat drones, in what could become a major shift in the country’s traditionally limited armed-uncrewed-aircraft capabilities.

evidenceRecords.text: Airbus and Kratos Defense & Security Solutions have completed the first flight of the U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft, a Europeanized version of the XQ-58A Valkyrie , advancing their bid to deliver a combat-ready system to Germany by 2029.

The flight comes as the German Air Force, or Luftwaffe, moves toward acquiring a new class of jet-powered combat drones, in what could become a major shift in the country’s traditionally limited armed-uncrewed-aircraft capabilities.

The ride of the Valkyrie With the successful first flight of the Airbus U740 Valkyrie in Europe, we are one step closer to introducing an operational uncrewed Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) to the German and other European Armed Forces.

The flight achieved all… pic.twitter.com/S2sFrtdmGA — Airbus Defence (@AirbusDefence) October 12, 2026 The flight took place at an unnamed test facility in northern Europe, Airbus announced on October 12.
The aircraft conducted a rocket-assisted takeoff, maneuvers at different altitudes, and flight at speeds of up to Mach 0.8.
The U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft is prepared for launch.

Airbus The next phase will introduce Airbus’ Multi-platform Autonomous Reconfigurable and Secure (MARS) mission system, which is intended to provide the aircraft’s European-controlled software and mission-management architecture.
Airbus says MARS will support autonomous operations and coordination between multiple uncrewed aircraft while retaining human oversight of critical decisions.
The U740 is based on Kratos’ American-developed XQ-58A , an uncrewed aircraft designed as a relatively affordable combat platform.
The U740 Valkyrie on its launch trailer.
Airbus Published performance figures for the U740 include a maximum takeoff weight of around 3,000 kilograms (6,600 pounds).
A U.S. Marine Corps XQ-58A Valkyrie conducts a test flight with a U.S. Air Force F-16.

The South Carolina-based startup Powerus unveiled a fully autonomous version of its Guardian interceptor on Monday at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting.
Brett Velicovich, the company’s president and co-founder, said in an interview with Military Times that logical product upgrades have been key to the company’s success.

“When you go to Ukraine, most of the interceptors, believe it or not, are manually controlled,” he said, explaining that Ukrainian operators are highly skilled at finding and stopping one-way attack drones in the air. “And that’s great for Ukraine, where you could probably throw a rock and hit a drone pilot.”
The problem with the government’s initial thinking, according to Velicovich, was that Ukraine has a “proper drone army,” as the country has “entire brigades that are pilots.
So those guys have extreme combat experience in knowing how to take a drone and send it into another drone.
In other countries, they don’t.”

With that understanding, Velicovich explained how Powerus provided the U.S. with the Guardian 1 — modeled after manually controlled Ukrainian drone interceptors — to the semi-autonomous Guardian 2, which, when paired with a radar to detect threats, will launch the interceptor in the direction of a drone.
He explained that when the radar cues it, the system launches in the direction of the threat and can detect and strike using artificial intelligence and navigation systems.
Velicovich credits this strategy, which he and his team derived from first-hand experience in the military and using drones in combat, to the company’s recent success.

items.title: U.S. Navy to Integrate LRASM into USAF’s B-52 Strategic Bombers
items.originalTitle: U.S. Navy to Integrate LRASM into USAF’s B-52 Strategic Bombers
items.summary: The U.S. Navy announced plans to contract Lockheed Martin to integrate AGM-158C Long-Range Anti-Ship Missiles (LRASM) on the Air Force’s B-52 strategic bomber. This is the latest development from the U.S. military this year to enhance and showcase its aerial maritime strike capabilities. With its range and payload capacity, a B-52 Stratofortress equipped with LRASM can take off with a payload of 20 missiles. This capability, combined with the strategic bomber’s immense range, could prove crucial in a potential conflict against China.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Navy announced plans to contract Lockheed Martin to integrate AGM-158C Long-Range Anti-Ship Missiles (LRASM) on the Air Force’s B-52 strategic bomber.
With its range and payload capacity, a B-52 Stratofortress equipped with LRASM can take off with a payload of 20 missiles.
This capability, combined with the strategic bomber’s immense range, could prove crucial in a potential conflict against China.
Last Wednesday, Naval Air Systems Command released its intent to award Lockheed Martin for work to integrate LRASM with the B-52.
The contract will involve associated testing, missile software updates and test asset repair.
The Air Force has already integrated the munition of which LRASM is derived from, the AGM-158 Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missile (JASSM), across its bomber and fighter fleets.
B-52 and B-1 fleets have extensively deployed the missile during the U.S.-Iran War, according to Pentagon media.
The U.S. Navy plans to field LRASM against enemy warships in a future high-low munitions mix.
This is the latest development from the U.S. military this year to enhance and showcase its aerial maritime strike capabilities.

According to a Tailhook 2026 presentation, the stealthy long-range cruise missile and the low-cost Blackbeard High-Speed Long Range Maritime Strike Weapon will be key components for the future carrier air wing.

items.title: How exposed is Saudi Arabia? Yemen's Houthis scale up drone and missile attacks
items.originalTitle: How exposed is Saudi Arabia? Yemen's Houthis scale up drone and missile attacks

The defense giant unveiled the PAC-3 Edge this Friday and debuted it at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., today.

evidenceRecords.text: The latest iteration of Lockheed Martin’s PAC-3 family of missile interceptors is designed to bring extreme agility to bear against a diverse array of missile threats, Defense News learned.
The defense giant unveiled the PAC-3 Edge this Friday and debuted it at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., today.

It’s capable of being launched from the containerized launchers that are being sought after domestically and internationally, as well as our HIMARS FLEX, which is the offense and defense configuration of our traditional HIMARS vehicle,” Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control Integrated Air and Missile Defense, told Defense News.
Lockheed in January announced a seven-year framework agreement to increase annual PAC-3 interceptor production from approximately 600 to 2,000.

Designed to defend against hypersonic and advanced missile threats, the unveiling of the PAC-3 Edge comes as the U.S. military’s reliance on costly interceptors against cheap munitions, particularly those deployed by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, has come under increased scrutiny over the past eight months.
The new PAC-3 Edge missile builds on the foundations of the PAC-3 MSE, Lockheed’s baseline missile, and pushes its abilities farther.

“This has additional attitude control motors that give it additional agility.” While the PAC-3 MSE uses a two-pulse solid rocket motor to speedily approach moving targets, the new system has multi-pulse motor designed by Northrop Grumman.
The company intends to begin testing the PAC-3 Edge in 2027 and have it ready to deploy by 2031, although Lockheed aims to have it ready earlier, Reynolds added.

The companies said that the new agreement reflects a joint commitment to open architectures, rapid integration and commercial manufacturing for systems that can be fielded at scale.

The agreement establishes collaboration across Echodyne’s C-UAS radar hardware and software systems and ACS’s Bullfrog robotic weapon station capabilities, and follows the recent announcement of each company’s award from the United States’ Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401) for Domestic Shield, the JIATF-401 C-UAS Marketplace and other C-UAS requirements.

“Bullfrog combines computer vision, autonomous control and precision robotics with existing weapon systems to detect, track, identify and engage unmanned threats,” Echodyne said in a 12 October press release.
The company’s radar track data will extend this capability with persistent airspace positional information.

EchoShield generates location and velocity data for a wide range of drone types and flight profiles, and the system’s open interfaces enables radar data to flow directly into Bullfrog and broader command-and-control (C2) platforms.
Echodyne’s MESA radar architecture delivers electronically scanned array capabilities.
Maritime operations are one focus of the collaboration, with EchoShield increasingly integrated aboard uncrewed surface vessels for maritime awareness and C-UAS missions.
Echodyne and ACS will continue integrated testing and participation in US defence department demonstration events designed to evaluate the combined system under representative operational conditions.
The companies expect these activities to inform further product integration and support customer requirements across fixed-site, mobile, expeditionary and maritime missions.

evidenceRecords.text: Anduril has developed a new range of lower cost interceptor missiles called Steelfin to take down a range of aerial threats.

“Steelfin is a family of highly-configurable, mass-producible surface-to-air interceptor missiles that has been engineered to deliver cost, volume, and capability overmatch across the modern threat spectrum, including cruise, ballistic, and hypersonic missile threats,” said the company in a press release.

“Built around a common two-stage architecture, Steelfin allows Anduril to configure interceptor performance for different missions while repurposing many of the same components, production processes, and architecture across the family of interceptors.

Steelfin is a two stage design, encompassing a first-stage booster and second-stage terminal interceptor, offering the flexibility required to align interceptor performance to each threat, said the company.
The first stage can accommodate different solid rocket motor boosters to meet specific range, performance, booster types, launch configurations, or packing density requirements.
The second stage uses a common terminal interceptor architecture, sharing the same baseline airframe, avionics, software, flight control system, and interfaces across all Steelfin variants.

“Open, modular interfaces between each of the subsystems in the terminal stage allow Anduril to integrate different seekers, mission systems, and other components without redesigning the entire missile.” “Steelfin delivers a diversity of effects to meet a diversity of threats.

Unlike legacy missiles that carry fixed, inflexible designs that are resistant to change, Steelfin offers a common interceptor architecture that produces a family of interceptor missiles, each of which can be configured for a specific mission.
That approach provides warfighters with the options required to appropriately match interceptor capability and cost with the specific threat.

items.summary: U.S. Army Helicopter pilots in the 101st Combat Aviation Brigade are evaluating a system designed to let them relieve themselves in flight. The brigade completed the Army’s first-ever helicopter test flights using the Advanced Inflight Relief Universal System , or AIRUS, at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, from Oct. 5 to 7. Aircrews from 1-101 Attack Battalion “No Mercy,” 6-101 Assault Helicopter Battalion “Eagle Assault” and 7-101 Heavy Lift Battalion “Eagle Lift” completed human-factors surveys, checked AIRUS for fit and tested its ability to let them relieve themselves in flight.

evidenceRecords.text: U.S. Army Helicopter pilots in the 101st Combat Aviation Brigade are evaluating a system designed to let them relieve themselves in flight.
The brigade completed the Army’s first-ever helicopter test flights using the Advanced Inflight Relief Universal System , or AIRUS, at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, from Oct. 5 to 7.

Aircrews from 1-101 Attack Battalion “No Mercy,” 6-101 Assault Helicopter Battalion “Eagle Assault” and 7-101 Heavy Lift Battalion “Eagle Lift” completed human-factors surveys, checked AIRUS for fit and tested its ability to let them relieve themselves in flight.

The brigade’s Holistic Health and Fitness , or H2F, team sought out AIRION, the aerospace medical systems company that developed AIRUS, to help reduce the number of pilots purposefully dehydrating themselves to limit the need for restroom breaks during missions.
Gena Baisa, lead dietitian for the 101st CAB H2F team, said per an Army release.

“So, we thought, how can we get a system specifically designed to allow them to use the bathroom in air so they can stay hydrated and optimize their performance?” Chief Warrant Officer 2 Collin McAllister, an AH-64 Apache pilot who tested AIRUS, said the system differs from previous systems that used bags containing coagulant, according to an Army account of the testing.

items.summary: Lockheed Martin has unveiled the PAC-3 Edge, a new interceptor that would represent the top tier of the U.S. Army’s Patriot air defense missile family. The missile is being developed to deliver greater performance against advanced threats than the current PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE), as the Army advances a competition for its next-generation interceptor. The PAC-3 Edge displayed at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention.

evidenceRecords.text: Lockheed Martin has unveiled the PAC-3 Edge, a new interceptor that would represent the top tier of the U.S. Army’s Patriot air defense missile family.

The missile is being developed to deliver greater performance against advanced threats than the current PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE), as the Army advances a competition for its next-generation interceptor.
The PAC-3 Edge displayed at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention.
Howard Altman The company says PAC-3 Edge will offer improved performance against increasingly challenging aerial threats, including advanced ballistic and hypersonic missiles.
The design builds on the PAC-3 MSE’s existing technology while incorporating a new seeker, an upgraded control system, and a more advanced solid rocket motor developed with Northrop Grumman.
In terms of appearance, PAC-3 Edge differs significantly from the PAC-3 MSE.
An overview of the improvements found on the PAC-3 MSE variant over its predecessors.
The Army previously abandoned its Lower-Tier Future Interceptor (LTFI) program in 2024, citing cost concerns, and instead emphasized incremental improvements to the existing PAC-3 MSE.
A PAC-3 interceptor seen at the moment of launch.

U.S. Department of Defense A More Capable Patriot Interceptor PAC-3 Edge is intended to preserve the advantages of the existing PAC-3 family while improving the missile’s ability to engage targets at longer ranges and higher altitudes.

Tim Cahill, president of Missiles and Fire Control (MFC) for Lockheed Martin, told TWZ that the same seeker technology that will be used in PAC-3 Edge will also find its way into future offensive and defensive systems going into the future.

To ensure greater agility, Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD) at Lockheed Martin, explained that the new missile adds a greater number of more capable attitude control motors (ACMs), compared to the PAC-3 MSE.

IonQ CEO Niccolo de Masi said the acquisition aims to help customers address growing cybersecurity risks associated with AI and quantum computing. IonQ has agreed to buy cybersecurity company Elisity in an all-stock deal worth up to $1.3 billion, expanding its security business as advances in quantum computing and artificial intelligence raise concerns about cyberattacks.
The transaction includes up to $150 million in additional payments tied to Elisity’s future performance, executives told The Wall Street Journal .
IonQ Chairman and CEO Niccolo de Masi told the newspaper that the acquisition reflects his expectation that companies will need stronger defenses as both technologies become more powerful.
“With Elisity and its team as part of IonQ , we will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure and enterprise networks throughout the transition to the quantum era.
IonQ is offering its customers a vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform across quantum computing, networking, sensing and cybersecurity.

Just as adding SkyWater Technology expanded IonQ’s capabilities in chip design, fabrication and packaging, Elisity will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to our quantum security strategy and will give IonQ a strong growth platform to serve customers and create value for our shareholders,” Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ, said in a statement .
The Elisity agreement follows IonQ ’s $1.8 billion deal earlier this year to acquire chipmaker SkyWater Technology, likely its largest acquisition to date.

items.summary: ROME — Italy is holding tests with MBDA to mount the European firm’s armaments on the new Astore Levante drone being built by Turkey’s Baykar and Italy’s Leonardo , the head of the Italian air force has said. The Italian air force is due to acquire six of the drones, which are derived from Baykar’s TB-3 and are being assembled in Italy by LBA Systems, a joint venture between Baykar and Leonardo.

evidenceRecords.text: ROME — Italy is holding tests with MBDA to mount the European firm’s armaments on the new Astore Levante drone being built by Turkey’s Baykar and Italy’s Leonardo , the head of the Italian air force has said.
The Italian air force is due to acquire six of the drones, which are derived from Baykar’s TB-3 and are being assembled in Italy by LBA Systems, a joint venture between Baykar and Leonardo.

The Astore Levante is due to carry Leonardo sensors, but at its unveiling at the Farnborough air show in July it was presented alongside Turkish armaments, including Roketsan’s MAM family of guided bombs and Baykar’s KEMANKES-1 mini cruise missile.
Speaking in Rome on Monday, Italian air force chief Gen.
“At the moment we have not made choices, the natural armament is Turkish but we also have activities with MBDA and small Italian industrial groups,” he said.
European certification is deemed a prerequisite for selling the drone in Europe.

The Italian air force will initially order three systems, each containing two drones, but Conserva said, “We will see if we go on to expand the capability.” The Astore Levant will replace the Predator MQ1 flown by the air force, Conserva added.
As well as being flown on ISR missions and providing armed support for troops, the drones will also be used for training drone pilots, he said.
Before the launch in July of the Astore Levante, the Italian navy said in April it was eyeing the TB-3 as a carrier-borne drone to fly off its Cavour carrier, which also hosts Italy’s F-35Bs.
Another TB-3 customer, Indonesia, is expected to base the drone on the Garibaldi, a carrier it has purchased from Italy.
Conserva spoke to reporters on Monday at a conference at the HQ of the Italian air force in Rome which gathered air force and industry officials to discuss the future of warfare.

items.title: One user interface, multiple autonomous systems: Forterra debuts OASIS-OneLink technology
items.originalTitle: One user interface, multiple autonomous systems: Forterra debuts OASIS-OneLink technology
items.summary: Defense tech company Forterra introduced a new platform on Monday at the Association of the United States Army conference in Washington that will allow service members to control different autonomous systems using one user interface. OASIS-OneLink builds upon Forterra’s OASIS-Fabric, a shared data network that allows unmanned machines to connect in communication-degraded environments where they can’t log onto a shared data grid.

evidenceRecords.text: Defense tech company Forterra introduced a new platform on Monday at the Association of the United States Army conference in Washington that will allow service members to control different autonomous systems using one user interface.
OASIS-OneLink builds upon Forterra’s OASIS-Fabric, a shared data network that allows unmanned machines to connect in communication-degraded environments where they can’t log onto a shared data grid.

“Requiring operators to start an integration process from scratch every time a new system is introduced is both inefficient and burdensome for the end user,” Phil Cotter, Forterra’s head of growth, told Military Times.
While Fabric provided a new way for machines to connect, OneLink provides a new way to control them.
New systems and pieces of technology come with their own operating systems and visual layouts, not unlike different computers or phones.

If a service member wants to control several different autonomous systems, or if a new one is introduced to the mix, they may have to learn a completely new user interface or remember several different ones while toggling between them.
But OASIS-OneLink would allow several different autonomous machines, potentially all from different companies, to be controlled using the same operating control framework, said Tuck.

The shared interface could also speed up the testing and evaluation phase before fielding new technology, since it would allow the Defense Department to focus on the performance of new autonomous systems and reduce time otherwise devoted to the tedious mastery of new controls.
The Army’s Joint Readiness Training Center has already begun using OASIS-OneLink to pilot unmanned systems, Forterra said.
Oasis-OneLink wasn’t the only shiny new toy the company showed off at AUSA.

The company unveiled a new autonomous ground vehicle that it created with Hypercraft, integrating its AutoDrive autonomous software platform to form a machine capable of carrying out high-risk missions without endangering soldiers’ lives.

evidenceRecords.text: Defense companies Vector and Nammo Defense Systems announced Monday at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting that they had expanded their partnership to integrate munitions into small drones for U.S. military use.
The companies first teamed up earlier this year to pair Nammo’s munitions with Vector’s unmanned aircraft.
The expanded agreement aims to scale that work to help address what the companies describe as a growing need for drones that can deliver more than just explosive payloads.

Andy Yakulis, Vector’s chief executive officer and co-founder, called the partnership “highly complementary” because together they produced a system that reflects “the realities of how warfighters will employ them.” “The battlefield is demanding unmanned systems that can do more than simply carry a payload,” he said, adding that their systems will be produced at scale and “continuously improved based on real-world requirements.” According to Vector’s website , the Utah-based company launched in 2024 with three veterans, including Yakulis, as well as the founder of Teal Drones, which was later
According to both companies, the device enables the safe integration and controlled use of compatible munitions.

Vector has a drone listed on the Defense Department’s Blue List, which includes unmanned aircraft systems that have undergone the department’s relevant assessment and approval process for military use.

The company also placed in the top five in the latest round of the Defense Department’s Drone Dominance program , a billion-dollar initiative to procure affordable small drones that can be manufactured at scale.

Andy Schreiner, the president and general manager of Nammo, said the “expanded agreement will benefit warfighters defending freedom globally” because it combines “Nammo’s proven expertise in munitions, energetics, and advanced manufacturing with Vector’s unmanned systems capabilities.” Nammo , a Norwegian defense manufacturer with U.S. operations headquartered in Arizona, specializes in ammunition, shoulder-fired weapons and rocket motors.

items.summary: Exail has started production of the Unmanned Mine Countermeasures Integrated System (UMIS) ordered by Indonesia, while also preparing to integrate third-party towed sonar and influence sweep systems selected by the country. Speaking to Naval News during the EURONAVAL 2026 Press Tour, Exail Mine Warfare Director David Barre said production has begun for the UMIS package announced in June 2025. The package will include four Inspector 90 unmanned surface vessels (USVs), along with Seascan mine-identification ROVs and K-Ster expendable mine-disposal systems.

evidenceRecords.text: Exail has started production of the Unmanned Mine Countermeasures Integrated System (UMIS) ordered by Indonesia, while also preparing to integrate third-party towed sonar and influence sweep systems selected by the country.
Speaking to Naval News during the EURONAVAL 2026 Press Tour, Exail Mine Warfare Director David Barre said production has begun for the UMIS package announced in June 2025 .
The package will include four Inspector 90 unmanned surface vessels (USVs), along with Seascan mine-identification ROVs and K-Ster expendable mine-disposal systems.
The UMIS will be deployed from the Indonesian Navy’s (TNI AL) two mine countermeasures vessels (MCMVs), KRI Pulau Fani (731) and KRI Pulau Fanildo (732) , built by Abeking & Rasmussen.
Exail said the systems can be produced relatively quickly.
Exail is also increasing its production capacity, including through a new facility which will soon break ground in southern France.
In addition, the company confirmed that Indonesia has selected towed sonar and influence sweep systems from European suppliers with whom Exail has previously collaborated.
Exail will integrate these systems into the UMIS package and provide the associated launch and recovery systems.
Speaking to Naval News during the EURONAVAL 2026 Press Tour, Exail Mine Warfare Director David Barre said production has begun for the UMIS package announced in June 2025.
The UMIS will be deployed from the Indonesian Navy’s (TNI AL) two mine countermeasures vessels (MCMVs), KRI Pulau Fani (731) and KRI Pulau Fanildo (732), built by Abeking & Rasmussen.
The company said it can, for instance, produce two K-Ster systems per day.

Earlier this year, Norwegian company Henriksen announced it would supply its Henriksen Multi Lightweight Influence Sweep (HEMLIS) system to the Indonesian Navy, marking the system’s first commercial sale outside Europe.
The HEMLIS will be integrated with the Inspector 90 USVs.
Exail said the Indonesian contract already includes the integration work for both third-party systems, as well as training for Indonesian personnel.

The company also said it expects further business from Indonesia, including possible orders for additional new systems and upgrades to the Indonesian Navy’s existing or legacy mine warfare equipment/platform.

items.title: WISeSat.Space Develops Post-Quantum Security for Satellite Communications
items.originalTitle: WISeSat.Space Develops Post-Quantum Security for Satellite Communications
items.summary: Insider Brief WISeSat.Space is developing a satellite communications and IoT security architecture that integrates post-quantum cryptography (PQC), digital identity, and cryptographic key management across connected devices, ground infrastructure, and future satellite platforms. The company plans to draw on SEALSQ’s QS7001 and QVault TPM platforms, which support NIST-standardized algorithms ML-KEM and ML-DSA, as it develops its Quantum Spatial Orbital Cloud.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief WISeSat.Space is developing a satellite communications and IoT security architecture that integrates post-quantum cryptography (PQC), digital identity, and cryptographic key management across connected devices, ground infrastructure, and future satellite platforms.
The company plans to draw on SEALSQ’s QS7001 and QVault TPM platforms, which support NIST-standardized algorithms ML-KEM and ML-DSA, as it develops its Quantum Spatial Orbital Cloud.

WISeSat.Space has access to nine active low-Earth-orbit satellites and targets a 100-satellite sovereign constellation by 2033, subject to financing, technical development, regulatory approvals, and launch availability.

PRESS RELEASE — WISeSat.Space (Nasdaq: SAIQ) (“WISeSat.Space” or the “Company”) today outlined its strategy to integrate post-quantum cryptography (“PQC”) into its next-generation satellite communications and Internet of Things (“IoT”) architecture, supporting the migration objectives established by U.S. Executive Order 14412, Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks.

The Company is developing a security architecture designed to protect communications, digital identities and satellite operations against both conventional cyberattacks and emerging quantum-computing threats.

“Security is a core differentiator in our strategy to build a satellite communications business serving governments, enterprises and critical infrastructure operators,” said Carlos Moreira, Founder and CEO of WISeSat.Space.

By integrating post-quantum technologies across connected devices, ground infrastructure and satellites, we aim to strengthen our competitive position, address demand for secure, sovereign communications and create long-term shareholder value.” Following its October 2026 business combination and Nasdaq listing, WISeSat.Space closed a $10 million PIPE investment led by SEALSQ to accelerate the development of its quantum-resilient space architecture.
Practical Applications Across Space and Earth WISeSat.Space is developing its architecture around several applications where communications security and long-term data protection are essential.

items.title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
items.originalTitle: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
items.summary: Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities". There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.

evidenceRecords.text: Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".

There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?
Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants
Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.
He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities."
"I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.
On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.
Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".

When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".

items.title: Mangroves and mud: Inside the Army jungle school’s notorious ‘Green Mile’
items.originalTitle: Mangroves and mud: Inside the Army jungle school’s notorious ‘Green Mile’
items.summary: The soldiers, some wearing days-old green face paint, had congregated amongst the moist fauna to complete their final task in the U.S. Army’s Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama: The Green Mile. The notorious event — in the thick of Panama’s “Green Hell” — is the 18-day course’s culminating exercise, testing participants’ newly learned jungle maneuver techniques, survival measures and fighting skills. By that point in the course, the soldiers had run a days-long jungle reconnaissance and attack operation.

evidenceRecords.text: The soldiers, some wearing days-old green face paint, had congregated amongst the moist fauna to complete their final task in the U.S. Army’s Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama: The Green Mile.

The notorious event — in the thick of Panama’s “Green Hell” — is the 18-day course’s culminating exercise, testing participants’ newly learned jungle maneuver techniques, survival measures and fighting skills.
By that point in the course, the soldiers had run a days-long jungle reconnaissance and attack operation.
The course in 2025 returned to Panama at Base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, formerly known as the U.S. Army’s Fort Sherman, decades after it was originally shuttered.
The new course is a joint U.S.-Panamanian partnership, with Panamanian instructors leading lessons on jungle survival.
Squads in the September course had participants from across the U.S. force, including those from the Army, Marine Corps and Space Force.
Some squads had Panamanian soldiers.
That portion of the field exercise was complete, and perhaps to the howler monkey’s dismay, so were the soldiers’ attempts to stay quiet.
With staggered start times, each squad took off running down a soggy, uneven path.
Other countries, such as Colombia, have expressed interest in sending soldiers in the near future.
In classes with Panamanian students, instruction is given in English and Spanish.
When the course is English-only, the duration shrinks to 12 days, but without partners, officials say U.S. students can miss out on opportunities to connect with other forces.

The capability will be deployed across Denmark, integrating Systematic’s SitaWare Suite with sensor information, operational data and personnel to support the detection, assessment and response to potential drone threats, according to the company in a press release.

evidenceRecords.text: Systematic has been awarded a contract by the Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation (DALO) to deliver an AI-ready command-and-control (C2) capability for counter-drone defence.

The capability will be deployed across Denmark, integrating Systematic’s SitaWare Suite with sensor information, operational data and personnel to support the detection, assessment and response to potential drone threats, according to the company in a press release.

“As part of the suite, SitaWare Headquarters will provide an overview of counter-drone activity across sites and military domains, while SitaWare Insight will use AI-supported analysis of historical and near-real-time data to identify patterns, anomalies and potential threats,” said the company.
“In a September assessment, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) warned of an increased risk of Russian hybrid warfare activities against Western countries, including the use of drones.

The warning follows a series of incidents across Europe, including reported drone activity near Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany in August and Russian airspace violations involving NATO members, including Estonia, Latvia, Poland and Norway.

The new capability will integrate Systematic’s SitaWare software with Terma’s OSL counter-drone system contract announced earlier this summer, allowing sensor information to be brought into a common, operational picture in near real time.
The announcement comes as NATO accelerates efforts to strengthen counter-drone capabilities with the ability to adopt AI across defence.
It also supports multinational formations such as the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), enabling forces from different nations to operate together and share information seamlessly across domains.

items.title: Canadian UAVs DAA system supports BVLOS flights for Navy UAS
items.originalTitle: Canadian UAVs DAA system supports BVLOS flights for Navy UAS
items.summary: Canadian UAVs (CUAVs) said on October 6 that it deployed its Sparrowhawk ground-based detect-and-avoid (DAA) system to enable safe beyond visual line of sight flight operations of the Royal Canadian Navy’s (RCN) new CU-179 Peregrine remotely piloted aircraft system. From 24 August to 4 September 2026, Sparrowhawk fused airspace radar, ADS-B and AIS into a single, continuous air and surface picture of restricted airspace over the Strait of Georgia for CU-179 flights at the Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental and Test Ranges in Nanoose Bay, British Columbia.

evidenceRecords.text: Canadian UAVs (CUAVs) said on October 6 that it deployed its Sparrowhawk ground-based detect-and-avoid (DAA) system to enable safe beyond visual line of sight flight operations of the Royal Canadian Navy’s (RCN) new CU-179 Peregrine remotely piloted aircraft system.

From 24 August to 4 September 2026, Sparrowhawk fused airspace radar, ADS-B and AIS into a single, continuous air and surface picture of restricted airspace over the Strait of Georgia for CU-179 flights at the Canadian Forces Maritime Experimental and Test Ranges in Nanoose Bay, British Columbia.
Sparrowhawk holds a Transport Canada Pre-Validated Declaration, giving the RCN a validated DAA foundation for CU-179 operations without having to build a safety case from scratch.

During the deployment, Sparrowhawk detected a low-flying general aviation aircraft transiting the restricted area while transmitting no ADS-B, an aircraft that was visible to radar alone and would not have appeared in a cooperative-only airspace picture.
RCN personnel operated Sparrowhawk directly throughout flight operations, with six RCN operators trained on the system during the deployment.

CUAVs said the RCN deployment demonstrates a pathway for defence forces to access civilian airspace at scale, flying uncrewed aircraft alongside existing traffic without restricting or interrupting the airspace for other users.

The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.
A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.
Explosions were heard again in Riyadh on Monday night, with the Saudi-led military coalition saying a ballistic missile had been intercepted and destroyed.
A Houthi spokesperson said the group had again targeted the airport.
Meanwhile, Qatar Airways has said it will temporarily suspend flights to Riyadh and the north-eastern city of Dammam.
Etihad Airways said it had cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to "regional disruption".

On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.

items.originalTitle: This Is Our First Look At The Wolf Armored Fighting Vehicle That Aims To Replace The Bradley
items.summary: General Dynamics Land Systems (GDLS) has offered the first official look at its proposal to replace the U.S. Army’s Bradley Fighting Vehicles, called the Wolf. The Wolf is one of two designs competing to become the Army’s future XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle (MICV). GDLS is showing the one-eighth-scale model of Wolf, seen at the top of this story and made by a company called KiwiMill , at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention, at which TWZ is in attendance .

evidenceRecords.text: General Dynamics Land Systems (GDLS) has offered the first official look at its proposal to replace the U.S. Army’s Bradley Fighting Vehicles, called the Wolf.
The Wolf is one of two designs competing to become the Army’s future XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle (MICV).

GDLS is showing the one-eighth-scale model of Wolf, seen at the top of this story and made by a company called KiwiMill , at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention, at which TWZ is in attendance .
It has already been established that Wolf is a further evolution of the GDLS’ Griffin III design, which was first shown publicly at AUSA back in 2018.
Griffin III was derived from the ASCOD 2 infantry fighting vehicle, for which Spain was the launch customer, and which is now entering service in Latvia.
The U.S. Army’s now-cancelled M10 Booker ‘light tank’ and the British Army’s much-troubled Ajax are also members of this broader family of armored vehicles.
GDLS/KiwiMill The design of the Wolf, at least based on the model, is substantially different from the earlier Griffin III demonstrator.

items.title: In Step Toward Quantum Networking, Penn Study Finds Quantum Light Pattern Can Survive Loss of Entanglement
items.originalTitle: In Step Toward Quantum Networking, Penn Study Finds Quantum Light Pattern Can Survive Loss of Entanglement
items.summary: University of Pennsylvania researchers have used a photonic chip to transfer a winding pattern in quantum light that survived noise even after entanglement disappeared, which they say could help develop quantum networks. The team suggests this experiment could be an initial step on the path toward more resilient links between those extremely sensitive quantum systems.

evidenceRecords.text: University of Pennsylvania researchers have used a photonic chip to transfer a winding pattern in quantum light that survived noise even after entanglement disappeared, which they say could help develop quantum networks.
The team suggests this experiment could be an initial step on the path toward more resilient links between those extremely sensitive quantum systems.

The study, published in Nature Physics , demonstrates a way to create and manipulate quantum skyrmions, which are structured patterns in light whose overall winding can remain stable even as their underlying quantum state deteriorates.
In this case, these light patterns can retain their overall winding even as noise degrades their quantum state.
According to the study, the silicon nitride chip combined components that generated photon pairs, routed the photons and shaped the light into skyrmions.

Connecting quantum computers and other quantum devices is challenging because noise — which can include anything from heat to cosmic rays — can weaken the delicate relationships that carry quantum information, making it difficult to move that information reliably between systems.
The scientists preserved a particular measurable property of the light, rather than showing that an entire quantum state could be transmitted intact after entanglement was lost.
They point out that the experiment does not establish a practical advantage for quantum state transfer.

A Pattern That Holds Its Shape A photon, which is a particle of light, has a quantum state that can include polarization — the orientation and motion of light’s electric field — and spatial properties associated with how the light’s wavefront is arranged.
In these skyrmions, the orientation of light’s electric field changes from place to place, forming a winding pattern.

items.originalTitle: UK retains early access to test latest US AI models
items.summary: Britain will retain early access to the latest artificial intelligence models for safety testing, the country's AI minister confirmed Monday, following reports that the White House had restricted the U.K.'s access. Concerns about AI safety have escalated in recent months after models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic were involved in security incidents during testing, piling pressure on governments to regulate the technology. UK retains early access to test latest US AI models (2026, October 12)

evidenceRecords.text: Britain will retain early access to the latest artificial intelligence models for safety testing, the country's AI minister confirmed Monday, following reports that the White House had restricted the U.K.'s access.

Concerns about AI safety have escalated in recent months after models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic were involved in security incidents during testing, piling pressure on governments to regulate the technology.

"We have been working closely with the U.S. government ... to retain access for Britain's AI Security Institute to the most powerful AI models before they are released," AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said in a speech in London.

Narayan said Britain's AI Security Institute, established in 2023, had been granted access to Google's most powerful AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, which has not been released publicly over safety concerns.

items.originalTitle: Sound waves come in quantum jumps

evidenceRecords.text: The move is part of the nascent command’s mission to build a “theater Army,” Ryan said, above and beyond the largely partner training and disaster response missions its U.S. Army North and South predecessors maintained.

The move is part of the nascent command\u2019s mission to build a \u201ctheater Army,\u201d Ryan said, above and beyond the largely partner training and disaster response missions its U.S. Army North and South predecessors maintained.\u00a0

\u201cFuture multinational training events will shift away from strictly relationship-building engagements toward operations directly targeting drug cartels and designated terrorist organizations,\u201d he said.
Ryan said the review was directed by SOUTHCOM\u2019s commander, Marine Gen. Frank Donovan, \u201cto better align with current federal priorities and strategy.\u201d

Those priorities include the latest National Defense Strategy\u2019s shift that puts defending the homeland at the top of the list, with the Western Hemisphere as the Pentagon\u2019s priority theater, a concept dubbed the \u201cDonroe Doctrine.\u201d
That focus on SOUTHCOM gave rise to the administration\u2019s strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean and the raid to capture Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.\u00a0

\u201cMake no mistake, these designated terrorist organizations operate as global financial networks, utilizing a resilient business model built to endure over decades unless targeted interventions actively disrupt their economic base,\u201d Ryan said.
At the same time, the Army is also beefing up its ability to do the legacy mission of crisis response in SOUTHCOM, Ryan said.
The service recently got approval to move more aviation assets and personnel down south, to help move people and supplies.
Ryan said the review was directed by SOUTHCOM\u2019s commander, Marine Gen.

items.originalTitle: Ukraine says Russia launched strikes hours after Donald Trump announced an 'energy ceasefire'
items.summary: Less than 24 hours after Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire," Ukraine reported Russian strikes in Kyiv, Kharkiv and Donetsk. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday said Russia carried out strikes, despite US President Donald Trump claiming a "ceasefire" had been agreed over the weekend. Trump announced unilaterally on social media on Sunday evening that "both parties" had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" which was "effective immediately."

There was no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from Moscow and Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's claim that the ceasefire was "news for me."

On Monday morning, Zelenskyy told the annual Warsaw Security Forum that there had been "Russian ​violations of the energy ​ceasefire announced President Trump" overnight, while the mayor of the northeastern city of Kharkiv reporting at least 12 injuries in attacks on energy facilities.
"It was clear that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not read Truth Social," Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.

"If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then it must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people," he said via video link, adding that he learned about the apparent ceasefire through the media.

"If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond."

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said on Monday at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg that the bloc would "welcome the energy ceasefire if it holds" but added: "We haven't yet seen that Russia will also stick to it."

French President Emmanuel Macron also insisted that a "real ceasefire" be "respected by both sides" but said: "I ​have ⁠not noted, over the last 48 ⁠hours, ​any energy ceasefire coming from the Russian side."
The Russian government said on Monday that President Putin would only consider a ceasefire for a single day in the event that Ukraine intended to hold a presidential election.

items.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
items.originalTitle: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
items.summary: Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation.

evidenceRecords.text: At a glance StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether
A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student.
Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits.
Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning.
Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners.
The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage.
Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation.
Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input.
They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question.
In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance.
The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move.

The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source.
All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup.
Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition.
The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions.
The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition.
It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization.
The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors.
StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research.

The archbishop who oversees the spiritual care of Catholics serving in the US military condemned the Pentagon’s proposed plans to livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan later this year.
He joins other Catholic leaders in speaking out against the death penalty and the live stream plans.
Hasan, an army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in 2009 at Fort Hood in Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on 3 December.
Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, announced last week that Hasan’s execution would be public, and the Pentagon later confirmed it would be livestreamed.
The crime committed by Hasan “was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?” Broglio asked.

“The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio added. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world?”

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Air Force will buy data collected by WindBorne Systems‘ fleet of autonomous weather balloons under a new contract that could be worth nearly $50 million to the startup.

WindBorne currently has about 700 weather balloons flying around the globe, collecting atmospheric sensor readings that the company sells to customers and also feeds into its own AI weather forecasting model.
WindBorne, founded in 2015 and based in Redwood City, California, is one of the first organizations to directly feed empirical data into a deep-learning weather model.

The company has worked closely with the U.S. government, particularly the National Weather Service and the U.S. Air Force and Navy, but this is the single-largest contract the company has participated in.
The contract is worth up to $49 million, but the Air Force pays only as it needs data.
It can place orders for specific regions at specific times.
So far, it has ordered $1.7 million worth, and executives expect more orders to follow.

“This is largely a vehicle through which continued growth of the constellation can be supported, as well as some work on research and development to continue to improve the hardware and performance of the balloons,” WindBorne co-founder and CTO Andrey Sushko told TechCrunch.

He added that the contract, which was awarded without competitive bidding, is “a determination by the government that for this capability of collecting global data, we were the only company able to provide it in the way that met their needs for these operations.”
WindBorne CEO John Dean told TechCrunch in August that the company had raised a $37 million Series B round to continue scaling its business.

Earlier this summer, the company released the latest version of its forecasting model, WeatherMesh 6, which it says provides more accurate forecasts than the traditional model run by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which simulates the atmosphere using the laws of physics.
In August WindBorne became the first organization to send an unpowered flight system — one with no engine — to collect data in the eye of a typhoon.
The company maneuvers its balloons by adjusting their altitude, bleeding air, or dropping sand carried as ballast, to send the vehicles into winds that take them where they need to go.

evidenceRecords.text: Elsight wants to change that with a new positioning technology designed to help uncrewed systems determine their location even when GPS is unavailable, jammed, or spoofed. more…
GPS has become such a routine part of flying a drone that it’s easy to forget how vulnerable it can be.
Jam a satellite signal, feed a receiver fake coordinates, and an autonomous aircraft or ground vehicle could suddenly struggle to figure out where it is.
Elsight wants to change that with a new positioning technology designed to help uncrewed systems determine their location even when GPS is unavailable, jammed, or spoofed.
The Texas-based company has introduced a positioning capability that uses cellular network signals as an alternative source of location data.
The system is designed for autonomous platforms operating across air, land, and maritime environments, including places where satellite navigation cannot be trusted.
The timing is significant.
GPS jamming and spoofing have become growing concerns in military operations, with electronic warfare tools increasingly used to disrupt navigation and communications.
For drones and other autonomous vehicles, losing reliable positioning can complicate everything from route planning to mission execution.
There is also a practical advantage for existing customers.
The positioning capability is integrated into Elsight’s Halo platform, which combines cellular, satellite, and radio-frequency links to maintain connectivity for uncrewed systems.
Existing Halo customers can access the new feature through software or a feature unlock, without installing additional hardware.
There is one important distinction, however: this isn’t a universal replacement for GPS or a guarantee of uninterrupted positioning everywhere.

By using cellular infrastructure as an independent reference and checking GPS against it, Elsight is betting that resilience can be added without making autonomous platforms significantly more complicated.

evidenceRecords.text: The Tigray conflict puts the UAE’s backing of Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s diplomatic role under scrutiny.

Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – As renewed fighting in Ethiopia’s Tigray region threatens to destabilise the Horn of Africa, public backing by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of Ethiopia’s federal government and Saudi Arabia’s record of regional diplomacy are drawing scrutiny.
Both Gulf powers have strategic interests in the Horn of Africa, but their roles differ.

The UAE has publicly backed Ethiopia’s government while Saudi Arabia has previously helped broker an Ethiopia-Eritrea rapprochement and was reported to have offered to mediate between the two countries in 2025.
Saudi Arabia has yet to publicly announce its position on the latest fighting in Tigray.
Saudi Arabia has previously sought to mediate between Ethiopia and Eritrea.
In November 2025, Chatham House reported that sources said Riyadh had offered to mediate between the two countries amid rising tensions over maritime access and regional security.
The kingdom’s broader regional alignment also matters.
An August 2026 analysis by the Soufan Center described Saudi Arabia and Egypt as backing Eritrea in opposition to Ethiopia’s ambitions for Red Sea access.
The UAE’s close ties with Addis Ababa could provide a channel for diplomatic engagement while Saudi Arabia’s record of regional diplomacy offers a possible opening for renewed talks.
However, the available public evidence does not establish that either country is currently leading an initiative to contain the crisis.
The UAE and Saudi Arabia should not be cast as pursuing opposing strategies simply because one has publicly backed Ethiopia’s federal government while the other’s current position is less visible.
Their interests and diplomatic approaches differ, but the evidence does not show that either has decisive influence over the fighting.

evidenceRecords.text: Meta on Monday unveiled two new "frontier" artificial intelligence (AI) models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude.
"Muse Spark was our first family of models, and now Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier," CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X.

Zuckerberg has pushed Meta to compete with leading AI labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, over the past year or so amid a race to win over customers and diversify beyond advertising, from which it has historically derived most of its revenue.
In June 2025, the company made a $14 billion investment in Scale AI, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and poached its co-founder Alexandr Wang as part of the deal.
Zuckerberg subsequently made Wang the company's chief AI officer overseeing its newly formed division called Superintelligence Labs.

Wonder is Meta's first new model since April, when it launched a frontier model called Spark, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry.
The new models can be used in Meta's new personal agent app, known as Muse, for paid subscribers only for now.
Wonder is "our largest and most capable model yet" and "rivals the big (boys)," Wang posted on X, presumably referring to leading labs OpenAI and Anthropic.

In a blog post, Meta touted so-called benchmarking data from an independent firm called Artificial Analysis, which appears to show that Meta's newest Wonder models outperform its own previous models, Spark, as well as various models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.
Artificial Analysis' own website shows that Wonder is also among the most expensive models.
Meta has committed billions toward competing in the global race to dominate AI, despite growing concerns about safety and security.

items.title: Starlink India launch: Why Elon Musk is still waiting
items.originalTitle: Starlink India launch: Why Elon Musk is still waiting
items.summary: Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, has escalated his criticism of the delay in launching Starlink in India. Last week, he sarcastically referred to Mukesh Ambani, one of India's richest people and chairman of Reliance Industries, as "Prime Minister Ambani" and accused his supporters of protecting a monopoly. "Would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?" Musk wrote on X, arguing that the service could bring internet access to underserved communities across India.

evidenceRecords.text: Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, has escalated his criticism of the delay in launching Starlink in India.

Last week, he sarcastically referred to Mukesh Ambani, one of India's richest people and chairman of Reliance Industries, as "Prime Minister Ambani" and accused his supporters of protecting a monopoly.
"Would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?" Musk wrote on X, arguing that the service could bring internet access to underserved communities across India.
Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the opposition Indian National Congress, joined the discussion, writing: "Welcome to India, Elon.
Wait till you discover the other guy." Musk replied: "Thank you, Rahul.
This is indeed troubling."
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) accused Gandhi of championing Musk's interests, while party leaders defended the government's handling of the issue.
Speaking during the India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi last week, Reliance Jio chairman Akash Ambani declined to comment on Musk's remarks.
He said: "I have no comments to make.
We want to keep our heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Akash, Mukesh Ambani's eldest son, also noted that Jio was progressing on its own end-to-end indigenous satellite broadband technology stack.
Meanwhile, Starlink — despite securing key approvals and signing distribution agreements with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel — has yet to begin commercial operations in India.

evidenceRecords.text: Andrej Karpathy, co-founder of OpenAI and now at Anthropic, sees a widening knowledge gap in AI.
The article Anthropic's Andrej Karpathy says "the external world has seen the preview" of what AI can actually do appeared first on The Decoder .
OpenAI co-founder and now Anthropic researcher Andrej Karpathy describes a widening gap in how people understand AI capabilities.
Only about 20 million professionals in math and programming use frontier models for work, by Karpathy's estimate.
Roughly 5,000 people worldwide have access to internal frontier systems.
Andrej Karpathy, co-founder of OpenAI, describes a rapidly widening gap in how people understand AI capabilities.
While the public treats chatbots like a better Google search, internal frontier systems are already tackling tasks that would take top experts years to complete.
Karpathy breaks down the user base of large language models into four levels.
About six billion people, roughly 75 percent of the global population, have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
Another one to two billion are casual users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products who treat them "a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc."
Even many professionals outside of math and code fall into this tier.

Executives and people in similar roles spend most of their time talking to other people, so "while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract," Karpathy writes.
The third tier covers an estimated 20 million people, about 0.2 percent of the world's population.

These are professional users of frontier-grade LLMs in math and code who see firsthand that "large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt." Karpathy lists "building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries" as examples.
"The external world has seen the preview," he writes.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Oxford physicists used a hybrid quantum computer combining qubits and quantum oscillators to observe the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a simulation of interactions between matter and gauge fields.
Encoding magnetic flux in entangled qubits caused destructive interference between two paths around a simulated loop, completely suppressing a matter particle’s tunnelling.
The study demonstrates how hybrid quantum systems can simulate fundamental interactions that become increasingly difficult to model on classical computers.

The effect is a quantum phenomenon in which a particle can acquire a measurable phase by travelling around a magnetic flux, even though it never passes through a region where a magnetic field is present.
The result demonstrates how hybrid quantum systems can be used to simulate interactions between matter and gauge fields that become increasingly difficult to model on classical computers.
Oxford physicists used a hybrid quantum computer combining qubits and quantum oscillators to observe the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a simulation of interactions between matter and gauge fields.

PRESS RELEASE — Physicists in the Department of Physics, University of Oxford, have used a hybrid quantum computer, formed by qubits and quantum oscillators, to observe the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a quantum simulation.
The paper has been published in Nature Physics.
In classical, everyday physics, the motion of a charged particle is determined locally by the electric and magnetic fields it encounters.
Quantum mechanics allows a more subtle effect.

In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle travelling around, rather than through, a region containing a magnetic field would still pick up a measurable trace of that field’s presence.
This became known as the Aharonov–Bohm effect, and it was later confirmed in experiments with real electrons.
Physicists are now interested in seeing the effect emerge in a different setting: lattice gauge theories.
These are mathematical frameworks used to describe interactions between matter and gauge fields, including important models in particle and high-energy physics.

The article Meta's new frontier model Muse Wonder Full breaks into the AI top tier appeared first on The Decoder .
Meta's two new models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, close the gap to the leading frontier models.
Meta released its frontier model Muse Wonder in two variants, and both land among the best AI models available.
Muse Wonder Full scores 56 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3, while Muse Wonder hits 52.
Its predecessor, Muse Spark 1.3, sat at 48 points, which makes this a significant jump from what was a mid-tier model.
The biggest gains show up in agentic evaluations, tests that measure how well an AI model can handle complex tasks on its own.
On Terminal-Bench 4.0, performance jumped from 33 to 57 percent.
Muse Wonder Full places in the top three on six out of ten benchmarks overall, a strong result for Meta, which seems to have recovered after a weaker stretch with its open Llama models.
Both models support a one-million-token context window and accept text, images, video, and audio as input.
Muse Wonder is available through Meta's API and Muse Code, while Muse Wonder Full is currently limited to Muse Code users.
Muse Wonder will soon power the Muse app as well, starting with paying subscribers.
Over time, Meta plans to build specialized models from it for all users.
Both models show big improvements in coding.
Muse Wonder Full hits 68 points on the Coding Agents Index, tying Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5.
On the AA-Omniscience knowledge test, Muse Wonder Full manages only 30 points, and Muse Wonder gets 25.
Muse Wonder Full cuts its hallucination rate from 33 to 23 percent compared to its predecessor, the second-lowest among all models scoring at least 45 index points.
The company says Muse Wonder Full does better than expected on unfamiliar tasks that weren't part of training optimization, and credits this to a stronger base model.
On the Vals AI Index, Muse Wonder Full (Max) debuts at fifth place and beats all OpenAI models, according to Vals AI.
On ProofBench, a private benchmark for mathematical proofs, Muse Wonder Full solves 94 out of 100 problems, up from 58 for its predecessor.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at KAIST, TDS Innovation, Hanyang University, UNIST , et al. published a technical paper titled “Spatially deterministic nucleation of 2D semiconductors by etching flux.” Abstract Excerpt: “Nucleation control is fundamental to semiconductor deposition, governing when, where and how crystalline materials form.
Conventional strategies can regulate nucleation density and, through area-selective growth, confine deposition to designated regions.

However, they generally do not determine where an individual nucleus forms within the growth regions, leaving even single-nucleation events spatially stochastic and limiting deterministic construction of crystalline materials.
Here we report etching-flux-mediated single-centred nucleation of two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors to deterministically localize a single nucleation event.” Find the technical paper here .
