evidenceRecords.text: Conflict and drought are increasing the risk of famine across Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, warns a global food crisis monitor.

“An El Nino-induced drought, affecting roughly half of the country, is compounding the impacts of conflict and displacement, reducing food availability, driving up prices and affecting livelihoods,” the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said on Monday in a statement.

Sudan’s war erupted in April 2023 when tensions between the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), escalated into open fighting in the capital, Khartoum, before spreading across the country.
The conflict has killed at least 150,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the actual toll is likely higher.
About 13 million people have been displaced.

evidenceRecords.text: Research published in the International Journal of Continuing Engineering Education and Life-Long Learning suggests that artificial intelligence is increasingly moving beyond technical automation to train engineers in ethical decision-making.
The work suggests this could address a critical gap in the Industry 4.0 era.

According to the new research, an AI-driven framework utilizing natural language processing (NLP), knowledge graphs and deep reinforcement learning can tailor ethics and professional competence training to individual engineers.
By analyzing engineering case studies against ethical guidelines and tracking user progress through dynamic learner profiles, the system might deliver personalized, adaptive teaching.

The researchers' tests on public datasets showed that their system outperformed traditional lecture-based methods, could predict professional competence and could substantially increase interactive training.
Engineering education has traditionally relied on conventional lectures.
That approach to teaching struggles to adapt to individual professional contexts or incorporate ethical reasoning.

Educational technology courses do exist online, but even they are typically optimized for simple performance metrics rather than measuring the multifaceted value of what is taught and ultimately learned.

evidenceRecords.text: The article Sakana AI's self-improving model gets better at solving and judging, but can't catch its own blind spots appeared first on The Decoder .
Sakana AI's MASS method lets one language model improve itself by solving tasks, judging results, and refining workflows without a stronger teacher model.
The study finds gains across all three roles, but shared blind spots can let errors pass as progress and feed into the next training cycle.
Researchers from Sakana AI and UC Berkeley have introduced "Multi-Agent Self-Supervision" (MASS), a method for recursive self-improvement (RSI).
A single language model handles the task, optimizes how the work gets done, and evaluates the results.
The model itself may therefore be the best available judge, even though it can miss its own mistakes when reviewing its work.
Using the same model to solve, check, and revise can reinforce those errors rather than correct them.

items.title: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
items.originalTitle: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
items.summary: Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model. Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding. According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

evidenceRecords.text: Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.
According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.

That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.
Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API.
Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.

In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”
To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark, which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks.
According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.
The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year.
Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.

items.originalTitle: SEALSQ Unveils VaultIC409 Secure Element for Post-Quantum Cryptography
items.summary: Insider Brief SEALSQ has unveiled VaultIC409, a secure element built on its QS7001 platform to support post-quantum cryptography in connected devices without requiring customers to redesign their existing hardware security architecture. VaultIC409 is designed to support ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), RSA and ECC, with a hardware Root of Trust, dedicated cryptographic acceleration and SPI connectivity.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief SEALSQ has unveiled VaultIC409, a secure element built on its QS7001 platform to support post-quantum cryptography in connected devices without requiring customers to redesign their existing hardware security architecture.
VaultIC409 is designed to support ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), RSA and ECC, with a hardware Root of Trust, dedicated cryptographic acceleration and SPI connectivity.

SEALSQ plans to demonstrate VaultIC409 using a TLS 1.3 application at Electronica from November 10–13, 2026, with engineering samples expected in Q2 2027; the underlying QS7001 platform is undergoing Common Criteria EAL5+ certification.

PRESS RELEASE — SEALSQ Corp (NASDAQ: LAES) (“SEALSQ” or “Company”), a company that focuses on developing and selling Semiconductors, PKI, and Post-Quantum technology hardware and software products, today unveils VaultIC409, a next-generation secure element designed to help hardware manufacturers address the growing cybersecurity challenges posed by quantum computing.

Built on SEALSQ’s QS7001 platform, which is currently undergoing Common Criteria EAL5+ certification process, VaultIC409 targets the same established markets as VaultIC408, giving existing customers a path to post-quantum security without redesigning their hardware security foundation.

VaultIC409 combines a hardware-based Root of Trust, cryptographic agility, dedicated cryptographic acceleration and Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) connectivity to provide a scalable foundation for the next generation of secure connected devices.
VaultIC409 gives our customers a direct path to post-quantum security on a certified platform they already know,” said Carlos Moreira, Founder and CEO of SEALSQ .

Extending our VaultIC family positions SEALSQ to support that transition across smart energy, industrial and IoT markets.” Demonstration and Availability SEALSQ plans to demonstrate VaultIC409’s capabilities through a TLS 1.3 application on its booth at the Electronica trade show (Hall C6 – 670) November 10 – 13, showcasing how hardware-based security, cryptographic acceleration and secure connectivity can support next-generation connected devices.
Engineering samples of VaultIC409 are planned to become available in Q2 2027, enabling customers and partners to evaluate the solution and begin integration activities for future product designs.

With VaultIC409, we are bringing together cryptographic agility, dedicated hardware acceleration and SPI connectivity to address the practical challenges of deploying Post-Quantum Cryptography in embedded devices,” said Gweltas Radenac, Product Marketing Director at SEALSQ .

“The ability to support RSA, ECC and PQC algorithms, combined with a hardware platform undergoing Common Criteria EAL5+ certification, gives manufacturers a foundation to provision identities, establish secure channels and anchor trust at runtime while preparing their products for the quantum era.” Built for Quantum-Safe Trust VaultIC409 extends SEALSQ ‘s VaultIC secure element portfolio with a security architecture designed for the transition toward quantum-resistant cryptography.

The secure element is designed to support emerging Post-Quantum Cryptography standards, including ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for quantum-resistant key establishment and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for digital signatures, alongside established cryptographic mechanisms required for hybrid security architectures.

items.originalTitle: Just 10 minutes of AI use may erode persistence on hard tasks
items.summary: Christian was part of a team behind a study that found that spending just 10 minutes relying on an AI tool significantly impairs our ability to focus and persist with difficult tasks. A preliminary draft made waves earlier this year, and the team presented the updated, peer-reviewed paper this week at the Conference on Language Modeling. evidenceRecords.text: Christian was part of a team behind a study that found that spending just 10 minutes relying on an AI tool significantly impairs our ability to focus and persist with difficult tasks.
A preliminary draft made waves earlier this year, and the team presented the updated, peer-reviewed paper this week at the Conference on Language Modeling.
To test how quickly people's focus and persistence plummeted, researchers designed a series of randomized controlled trials and recruited 1,222 participants online.

In the first experiment, which involved 354 participants, one group was tasked with solving 15 basic fraction problems without help, while another had ChatGPT open on the side to use for assistance or even to ask for the answer.
The group with AI access initially answered more accurately than the group without it.
Then, after 12 problems, researchers took away the AI tool.
Almost immediately, the people in that group stopped answering questions accurately.
Researchers then ran a third experiment with 201 participants and an SAT reading comprehension prompt.
The results echoed those from the fraction problems: When the AI tool was removed, persistence and accuracy dropped.
The findings backed up what anecdotes and surveys have increasingly found in recent years: An overreliance on AI for answers erodes our cognitive fitness.
When AI produces answers in seconds, we get used to that speed; anything that takes longer feels inefficient.
And relying on AI also removes what the team called "productive struggle," which can lead people to find their research strengths and passions.
Just 10 minutes of AI use may erode persistence on hard tasks (2026, October 12)

NATO is capable of carrying out this vision by implementing its “theory of victory,” a classified version of which was agreed upon by all 32 alliance members “about three months ago,” according to Grynkewich.

Grynkewich, who also serves as commander of United States European Command, did not say against whom, exactly, the alliance would fight, but the speech comes as European capitals have increasingly called out Russia for what they alleged are a string of sabotage cases across the continent.
Grynkewich said the incidents were making allied populations “a bit nervous.”
Grynkewich warned, “I want others to know who might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”
The theory of victory is structured around blocking, blunting and breaking an enemy — beginning with stymieing an initial attack and preventing an enemy advance by weakening it.
Drawing on the final part of the theory, said Grynkewich, “we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”

evidenceRecords.text: FN America introduced a new upgrade kit for the M240 machine gun on Monday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army, giving soldiers a way to mount modern optics on the legacy platform.

In a press release, Daryl Atkins, FN’s director for industrialized weapons, said the M240 Tactical Long Rail Upgrade Kit will allow military organizations to continue “taking advantage of the weapon’s proven performance while making it relevant for today’s combat requirements.” According to the company, the kit preserves the weapon’s original operating system and can be installed on new guns or used to upgrade existing weapons.

The kit includes: An 11-inch monolithic Picatinny top rail to accommodate night-vision and thermal optics, along with other components; An FN Side-Click feed cover designed to make one-handed operation easier; An FN Auto-Lock feed cover retention system that holds the cover open during loading, unloading and cleaning; A long, articulated carrying handle designed to accommodate full-size optics; An adjustable buttstock that allows soldiers to change the length of pull and cheek height or fold the stock for storage.

“With this upgrade kit, modern warfighters can achieve faster target acquisition, more consistent shooter fit and better management of optics, while military organizations can extend the value and relevance of currently fielded platforms,” Atkins said.

FN, the Belgian firearms manufacturer with operations in Virginia and South Carolina, has produced more than 100,000 M240 machine guns for the U.S. military since the 7.62mm weapon entered service in 1977.
However, last year the Army revealed through budget documents that it was investing $3.6 billion in a project, dubbed the Future Medium Machine Gun, or FMMG, to replace the legacy system.
The Army and Marine Corps are also pursuing separate efforts to modernize their squad-level weapons.

items.title: Quantum physicist Ignacio Cirac awarded 2026 Isaac Newton Medal and Prize
items.originalTitle: Quantum physicist Ignacio Cirac awarded 2026 Isaac Newton Medal and Prize
items.summary: The Spanish quantum physicist Ignacio Cirac from the Max Plank Institute of Quantum Optics in Garching , Germany, has won the 2026 Isaac Newton Medal and Prize for his “pioneering contributions that founded modern quantum information science, uniting profound theoretical insight, experimental vision, and exceptional scientific leadership shaping quantum physics and technology worldwide”. Presented by the Institute of Physics (IOP), which publishes Physics World , the international award is given annually for “world-leading contributions to physics by an individual of any nationality”.

evidenceRecords.text: The Spanish quantum physicist Ignacio Cirac from the Max Plank Institute of Quantum Optics in Garching , Germany, has won the 2026 Isaac Newton Medal and Prize for his “pioneering contributions that founded modern quantum information science, uniting profound theoretical insight, experimental vision, and exceptional scientific leadership shaping quantum physics and technology worldwide”.

Presented by the Institute of Physics (IOP), which publishes Physics World , the international award is given annually for “world-leading contributions to physics by an individual of any nationality”.
Born in 1965 in Barcelona, Spain, Cirac earned a PhD in physics from the Complutense University of Madrid in 1991.
In 2001 Cirac became director of the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics the US.
Cirac is best known for his work in the 1990s in which he co-developed a proposal for building a quantum computer using trapped ions with Peter Zoller from the University of Colorado at Boulder.

The “Cirac-Zoller” proposal provided an experimentally plausible route from the theoretical idea of a quantum computer to an actual machine with trapped ions remaining one of the leading quantum-computing platforms today.
He also showed how controlled quantum many-body systems can act as simulators to solve difficult problems in physics, chemistry, and materials science.

Cirac and collaborators also pioneered long-distance quantum communication, which included the idea of a quantum repeater that offers a way of distributing entanglement across distances despite losses and imperfections.
Cirac told Physics World that he is “deeply honoured” to receive the award.
“I’m very thankful to the people who have made this prize possible – it’s a team working for many years,” says Cirac.

Even without AlphaProof, it solved the nine Erdős problems, Google Deepmind reports.

"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said on Monday as EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a post on X that this was "the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war...More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
Although he could not attend the Luxembourg meeting due to a party conference in Berlin, Wadephul said: "The message is clear: Russia cannot and will not win this war."
However, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to imply that sanctions need to go even further as the conflict was set to enter its fifth bitter winter.

"This is the moment when the entire West...should show Russia and Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means," he told the Warsaw Security Forum, referring to EU sanctions. "That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia.
US President Donald Trump declared that there was an "energy ceasefire" in place between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend.
However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had no idea what Trump was referring to and that Russia had continued to target energy facilities unabated.

NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison This story is an update to the Antarctic sea ice feature in our World of Change series tracking long-term change on Earth’s surface through satellite imagery.
Because of this geography, sea ice has more room to expand during the winter.
Antarctic sea ice usually peaks in September, around the end of the Southern Hemisphere’s winter, and retreats to a minimum in February.
According to NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), Antarctic sea ice in 2026 likely reached its annual maximum extent on September 14 (above).
On that date, the ice covered an estimated 17.59 million square kilometers (6.79 million square miles), making it the third-lowest maximum on record.
The maps below show the average concentration of Antarctic sea ice for the month of September (left) and the following February (right) from 1990 to 2026.
For three consecutive years, from 2012 to 2014, satellites observed new record highs for winter sea ice extent.
These highs occurred while Arctic ice was in steep decline.
The climb came to an end in 2015, and significant decreases in sea ice around Antarctica started to occur in 2016.
There have since been years with small rebounds, but overall, Antarctic sea ice coverage has largely remained lower than normal.

items.title: Learning to Play Like a Pro: Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking for Humanoid Robots
items.originalTitle: Learning to Play Like a Pro: Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking for Humanoid Robots
items.summary: This White Paper provides roboticists and control engineers with a comprehensive overview of how motion planning and motion tracking can be decoupled to preserve professional athletic style in humanoid robots, and why adaptive, speed-aware control is essential for closing the gap between simulation and real-world deployment. What you will learn about: Why combining a professional athlete’s motion style with reliable task performance remains an open challenge in humanoid ball-sports robotics, and how separating a high-level planner from a low-level tracker addresses this trade-off.

evidenceRecords.text: This White Paper provides roboticists and control engineers with a comprehensive overview of how motion planning and motion tracking can be decoupled to preserve professional athletic style in humanoid robots, and why adaptive, speed-aware control is essential for closing the gap between simulation and real-world deployment.

What you will learn about: Why combining a professional athlete’s motion style with reliable task performance remains an open challenge in humanoid ball-sports robotics, and how separating a high-level planner from a low-level tracker addresses this trade-off.
How motion data extracted from broadcast video and motion-capture recordings can be reconstructed, retargeted, and physically corrected into reference motions a humanoid robot can safely track.
How this adaptive framework was validated across two humanoid platforms, including full-size, in-the-wild serving performed without any motion-capture system.
